flow_transcript_slices.question: Tell me about a time a child was having a really hard moment emotionally. What did you notice about what they were feeling, and how did you respond?
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q3 Attempt 1]
I usually notice each kid where they, let's say they were in my classroom for two, three weeks and you can see their behavior. They're pretty normal. And then randomly they start crying or wondering what's, what's going on. The example I can give you right now is a current client of mine, which I'm currently working with him. He's a foster kid. And I know there's a lot of changes in the foster program. So when I noticed that he's crying or banging his head, I do contact foster mom and I let them know, like, is there any changes, anything I am aware, like I can be aware of and we can work together. So whatever's going on there, I can figure out on my side or we can just communicate and how we can help the child. And usually that's. When foster mom will tell me, oh, well, his older brother, this is just an example. Didn't happen, but like went to back home and he stayed. So I have to figure out, okay, how can I do a curriculum or make them feel that it's okay. You'll see him again. You'll be okay, but he's just going through a lot of emotions. So I just had to figure out a way I can communicate with mom, see what I can do. And we can just figure it out together. So the child can still communicate. Continue to be comfortable. And.

flow_transcript_slices.question: Tell me about a time you felt overwhelmed at work with children present. What did you do to manage yourself?
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q4 Attempt 1]
I always, so my sister's a therapist and I know that when she's stressed a lot, she likes to just stop in her own time, right after work, just think of like a therapy. And then another thing that my sister always told me is always control your breathing, count your breathing and like always like coping mechanism where I don't really show that I'm stressed at work, but I know how to handle myself after work, like leaving that out. And one thing I do like to do is when I'm by myself, I go like, I don't know if you can see my screen, but I go to each finger and I just count and that's like a stress relief for me. But I learned a lot through my sister because she is a therapist and she deals with a lot, so I get a lot of coping from her. I think the only way I'll get stressed is that I do ask for help and my supervisor, there's no response or just me sitting down like, okay, what can I do? What can I do instead of getting the help that I need? And I do understand that sometimes supervisors are doing other things and they can't respond, but you really do need that help because you really want to follow guidelines and just not look bad. I guess if you, I don't know how to explain it, but that's the only thing I could think of, of the frustration sometimes at work. But other than that, I'm thinking of other ones, but it's mostly if I don't get the help from my higher ups. Figured it out myself, did emailed, I cc'd my boss and I let them know like the situation that was going on and what I did. And after that, I said, if you have any recommendation or any advice for me to follow up and see what I can do, my activities did not help with a child. I am open to more options, that's pretty much, I will have to figure it out myself and I usually do, but I do communicate what I did.

flow_transcript_slices.question: Tell me about a time something didn’t go as planned at work and your role in it. How did you handle the responsibility piece?
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q7 Attempt 1]
I can think of many. So I'll think of my preschool days where we, so kinder care has a curriculum that we all follow. And the two years old, they're not going to follow that curriculum. The two years old, their minds are barely expanding. They want to do everything they want. So it always, it's everything. It's never going to go as planned. So what I do is I try to do other activities or games where we try to do the activity for like 10 minutes and then we go for another one because they get bored very, very fast. So that's another thing where I have to explain to the director where the kids all over the place. So I have to make up more of an activity, but they want to follow the curriculum, which is not realistic. So I take it upon myself to make it more fun and just make sure that they, it goes smooth, but the curriculum is never going to go as planned. Another thing is when I did doing currently right now, the ABA, where you have a full set schedule, but it's not going to go as planned because it's going to be cancellation, either the child's sick or parents have doctor's appointment. So now I have to take it upon myself and see if I can either call someone else and put that spot that's empty or continue my day the way it is.
